title: The Weasel, The Goose, and The Cake Contest
markdown:
Professor Alistair Putterham was a weasel who liked things just so. His bookshop, The Gilded Quill, proved it. Books were not merely stacked. They were arranged by the exact shade of their covers, a rainbow that flowed from palest cream to deepest indigo. Sunlight through the wavy glass made patterns on the spines. Dust motes danced in the beams like tiny silent actors. Every morning, before the first customer thought about looking for a story, Alistair polished his glasses with a cloth as soft as a whisper. Then he straightened his carefully made waistcoat and got ready for the day.

Every day he took his proper walk from the shop to the busy bakery street. In summer that street became the heart of the Annual Whispering Willow Cake Contest, a mix of sweet smells, spices, and big dreams. Alistair’s entry was always the same, as sure as sunrise: a Lemon Verbena Tart. Light golden pastry. The gentle fresh smell of lemon verbena. One perfectly shined silver platter. It was simple. It was elegant. It was Alistair’s own calm, baked and served.

This year a new and very lively resident had arrived. Gwendolyn was a goose of a good size, with feathers as white as fresh snow and an even bigger love of life. She had decided, with the strong belief only a goose can have, that the bakery street was her own special path, and that any event happening there was an event she simply had to join. She did not just walk. She paraded, her webbed feet making a determined slap-slap-slap on the stones.

Until one day, Gwendolyn decided the cake contest needed more excitement. More goose.

Because of that, Alistair’s morning task of arranging his prize lemons on a pretty doily was rudely and noisily interrupted. A series of loud honks, like a foghorn with a tickle in its throat, announced her arrival. She flapped her grand wings and decided to help dust the entrance of The Whisked Wonders Bakery. Flour puffed out in huge soft clouds and covered everything nearby. Alistair, who had been adjusting a display of tiny globes in his doorway, was instantly powdered. He looked less like a dignified bookseller and more like a surprised sugar cookie that had tumbled into a flour bin. He blinked, set his glasses straight, and sighed a puff of white air. “How very unfortunate,” he murmured. Then he spent the next ten minutes brushing himself off, his neat world briefly turned into a fluffy mess.

Because of that, the air around the judging tent, usually vanilla, almond, and warm bread, now held a clear hint of goose feathers and slightly worried sugar. Alistair’s sensitive nose wiggled. His Lemon Verbena Tart sat on its silver platter like a jewel, a small island of order in the growing confusion. Gwendolyn, meanwhile, tried to taste-test a very tall meringue. With a shaky wobble and a soft sigh of sugar, it fell down in a sticky sweet pile. From his usual spot under the old oak, Jun the alpaca, Alistair’s good friend, made a quiet understanding hum. Sometimes life sent a bunch of geese your way. Jun’s hum was a soft rumble that meant a lot.

Because of that, the important moment arrived. The head judge, a round baker named Monsieur Pamplemousse, whose tummy was as round as the best brioche, was about to announce his decision on Alistair’s tart. Alistair stood tall, waistcoat smooth, paws clasped behind his back in a pose of perfect calm waiting. This was the result of all his careful work. Then Gwendolyn, full of boundless excitement, made her decision.

With a lot of determined waddling she made her way toward the judging table. Her bright dark eyes fixed on the shiny silver platter. She seemed to believe, with every part of her feathery self, that this perfect untouched creation was meant for her. As Monsieur Pamplemousse leaned in, forehead wrinkled with care, Gwendolyn lowered her head, ready for what she surely thought was a very important tasting. A shiver ran through Alistair’s whiskers all the way to his ears. A goose on his tart. His tart. The tart that showed order, dignity, and just the right amount of flavour.

He looked at the judges, their faces a mix of surprise and hidden giggles. He looked at Jun, who made another soft knowing hum that said, Here we go again. Then he looked at Gwendolyn, who regarded the tart with deep innocent hope, beak slightly open.

Until finally, Alistair Putterham, the picture of dignified control, the weasel who never spoke louder than a whisper, cleared his throat. The sound was quiet, but in the tense silence it cut through like a silver knife. “My dear judges,” he began, voice steady, though a tiny spark of annoyance flickered in his eyes, “and Gwendolyn. It appears we have forgotten a rather important, and perhaps very obvious, detail.” He paused, letting the words hang. “Geese, as wonderful as they might be for adding feeling — and I do admit her contribution has been memorable — are not usually known for their fine taste in delicate citrus flavours. Or for their ability to resist a perfectly flaky, buttery crust, for that matter.”

A silence fell. Then a soft chuckle started, a gentle wave that grew into a tide of happiness. Monsieur Pamplemousse’s large shoulders shook. His face turned a lovely pink. The simple truth had been said by the creature most dedicated to proper behaviour. Gwendolyn, startled by the shared sound, took a step back, head tilted, no longer quite so set on eating the prize tart.

“Indeed,” Alistair continued, a small dry smile touching his lips, a rare and precious sight. “I believe the main purpose of this important contest is to judge cakes, not to provide an early dessert for our very enthusiastic bird friends.” He moved his paw with the precision of a dancer. “And I daresay my Lemon Verbena Tart is still, quite wonderfully, perfect.”

The judges, wiping happy tears, burst into real laughter. Then, with a respect usually saved for very old books, they looked at Alistair’s tart. It was, of course, perfect. Without a single flaw. It won first prize, just as Alistair always knew it would, goose or no goose.

Ever since then, Professor Alistair Putterham still entered his tart every year. He still polished his glasses until they shone, and kept his dignified manner. But he always made sure to have a small pile of unsalted crackers ready, hidden neatly in his coat pocket, just in case Gwendolyn felt the strong need to add to the day’s atmosphere. And sometimes, when he heard a faraway familiar honk on the wind, he allowed himself a small knowing wink.
characters: Alistair Putterham (tidy weasel bookseller), Jun (alpaca friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
